<reason>A (CON) won the crux the debate narrowed to: both sides ended up agreeing the frontier should close, so the decision reduced to which instrument survives the weak state both conceded. A built the more coherent causal chain—prohibition under persistent demand manufactures a scarcity rent, weak maps make boundary-drawing pure discretion, and conduct enforcement punishes observable acts without enriching evaders. A answered both pressure questions directly and with principled distinctions (rules "fail differently"; "No" plus a constructive sequence), while B, pressed on the price mechanism in A's Q2, conceded in B4.3 that a hard stop raises the payoff to illegal clearing and offered only "visibility/costlier channel," which A turned ("illegality already happening doesn't get exposed because its margin grows—it gets better funded... not a wall, an auction"). B fought back well: the foregone-expansion reconciliation of the motion's concession was clean, non-fungibility blunted the cross-commodity leakage point, and "the last convertible hectare is the rent" plus "land race with better manners" were genuine hits on A's sequencing. But B never reconciled trusting the same captured state to hold a line whose value grows the harder it is drawn, its opening's own market-access lever was shown to run outside the state it distrusts, and its clipped Rebuttal 1 was a real execution cost. A's closing framed the agreed destination and decisive question more cleanly; B's closing asserted rather than re-established that only a hard stop honors it. Clear but competitive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's scarcity-rent exchange: A2.4 and pressure question Q2 forced B4.3 to concede that cutting legal supply raises the return to illegal clearing under admittedly weak enforcement; A4.4 and A5.3 converted that concession into the debate's decisive mechanism ("a rule that pays its violators is an auction"), which B's later "visibility" and rent-inversion answers never fully neutralized.</best_rebuttal>
